scores.evidence: Canary analysis needs metrics you can trust and a standardized deploy path, and neither exists until the earlier phases are done.
scores.rationale: Technical claims (OIDC, cosign, admission policies, Argo Rollouts, warn-first gates) are accurate, though shallow on hard parts like immutable digests and expand/contract migrations.

scores.evidence: Get one service all the way from commit to production first. Turn that into a reusable template. Then move the other services over in waves.
scores.rationale: Covers the sequencing request well with an explicit rationale and achievable scope, but runner cost, caching and change control are thin and exclusions are not explicit.

scores.evidence: Pull the pipeline out into versioned shared libraries or templates, one per archetype
scores.rationale: The phases fit together consistently; slight loose ends such as the gates being 'in parallel with Phase 5' while progressive delivery sits after Wave 2, and the data ownership of the deploy registry.

scores.evidence: Rollback works and has been tested on purpose
scores.rationale: Done-when criteria exist per phase and the hard pilot de-risks migrations early, but there are few measurable targets for build time, success rate or canary thresholds.

scores.evidence: I'm assuming a typical setup: containerized services, Kubernetes or similar, a small platform team (3–5 engineers)
scores.rationale: Key assumptions are stated and the plan says which answers change tool and wave choices, but the sensitivity analysis is limited and the 4–6 archetypes figure is a guess.

scores.evidence: Old pipelines left running quietly become permanent.
scores.rationale: It names domain-relevant failures (migrations left late, gate revolt, template sprawl, stalled migration), but the handling of secrets compromise, fork PRs, template breakage blast radius and CI outage is missing.

scores.evidence: SLOs for the platform itself (pipeline success rate, queue time, p95 build time)
scores.rationale: Platform SLOs, rollback, a deprecation policy and named team contacts appear, but there is no platform owner or on-call, no CI outage plan, and no template-change rollout procedure.

scores.evidence: Cost controls on runners and preview environments
scores.rationale: Cost is mentioned only in passing, with no estimate of build volume, hosted versus self-hosted runners, or scaling, apart from the platform team sizing.

scores.evidence: Make the core decisions: which CI engine, push-based deploys or GitOps (e.g. Argo CD), artifact registry
scores.rationale: It recognizes that core tooling decisions come first and puts the hard pilot early, but it does not weigh lock-in or exit paths, and the decisions are deferred to the team.

scores.evidence: Don't build every feature before anyone uses it
scores.rationale: Thin slice first, warn-only gates, and late progressive delivery are proportionate, and existing tools are used rather than a custom orchestrator.

scores.evidence: Done when: all 3 pilots run on shared templates with no copy-pasted pipeline code, and a new service can be onboarded in under a day.
scores.rationale: Each phase has an ordering rationale and checkable exit criteria, but tool choices are left open and there is no adaptation plan if the pilots disappoint.

checklist.evidence: List all 50 services: language, build tool, how and where each deploys... Group them into archetypes
run old and new pipelines side by side for about a week per service, then delete the old one
Build → unit tests → image → push → deploy to dev → promote to staging
Secrets management (Vault or a cloud secrets manager) and passwordless OIDC login from CI to the cloud
Image signing (cosign) and admission policies in the cluster (Kyverno or OPA)
Canary or blue-green releases (Argo Rollouts or Flagger), with automatic rollback driven by SLO metrics
Contract tests between services, plus integration tests in short-lived preview environments
Build caching, test sharding, quarantining flaky tests
Ephemeral CI runners that scale automatically
SLOs for the platform itself (pipeline success rate, queue time, p95 build time)
A basic deploy registry and audit log (which version is running where)

traps.evidence: Switching over: run old and new pipelines side by side for about a week per service
promote to staging → manual approval → prod
passwordless OIDC login from CI to the cloud
Each wave needs a named contact on every team being migrated.
which CI engine, push-based deploys or GitOps (e.g. Argo CD)

note: A sound, well-sequenced migration plan with a pilot, templates and parallel running, but thin on runner cost, caching targets, immutable artifact promotion, untrusted-build secret handling and change-control detail.
